name: Chiapas: Palenque & San Cristóbal
tagline: Jungle-wrapped Maya temples at Palenque, a highland colonial town with indigenous markets and cold clear mornings, and waterfalls and canyons in between.
highlight: The Temple of the Inscriptions rising out of the rainforest at Palenque, with howler monkeys calling in the mist.
shortDescription: Mexico's deep south: Palenque's sculpted Maya city in the jungle, the waterfalls of Agua Azul, the Sumidero Canyon and San Cristóbal de las Casas, a colourful highland town with living Tzotzil and Tzeltal Maya culture.
metaDescription: A Chiapas travel guide: Palenque's temples and jungle, Agua Azul and Misol-Ha waterfalls, the Sumidero Canyon, San Cristóbal de las Casas, indigenous markets, coffee and amber, when to go and a four-day plan.
nearestAirport: Tuxtla Gutiérrez (TGZ), about 1 hour to San Cristóbal; Palenque (PQM) has limited flights
knownFor: Palenque, Agua Azul, the Sumidero Canyon, San Cristóbal, Maya villages
goodFor: Maya ruins, jungle and waterfalls, indigenous culture, coffee, hiking

intro: Chiapas is Mexico's southernmost state, bordering Guatemala, and it is different in almost every way from the north and centre: greener, wetter, poorer and more indigenous. About a quarter of its people speak an indigenous language, mostly Tzotzil, Tzeltal and Ch'ol, and their villages, markets and festivals are among the most distinctive in the country.

Palenque, in the lowland jungle near the border with Tabasco, is one of the most beautiful Maya cities. Its temples, built in the 7th century under the ruler K'inich Janaab' Pakal, sit on terraces above the forest, and the Temple of the Inscriptions holds his tomb, discovered in 1952. Only a fraction of the city has been excavated, and the rest is covered by forest. UNESCO listed the site in 1987.

In the highlands, San Cristóbal de las Casas is a colonial town at 2,200 metres, of cobbled lanes, ochre churches and lively markets, with a strong artistic and backpacker scene. Between the two, the roads pass waterfalls at Agua Azul and Misol-Ha and, near Tuxtla, the Sumidero Canyon, whose walls rise a kilometre above the river. Chiapas has had periods of unrest, including the Zapatista uprising of 1994, and some areas are subject to warnings, so check your government's advice.

whyVisit.intro: Chiapas offers the most dramatic combination of jungle, ruins and living indigenous culture in Mexico.

points.title: Palenque
points.text: Ornate stucco reliefs, tall towers and a jungle setting make it the most atmospheric Maya ruin in Mexico.

points.title: Waterfalls
points.text: Agua Azul's turquoise cascades and Misol-Ha's 35-metre fall are among the prettiest in the country.

points.title: San Cristóbal
points.text: A colonial highland town with markets, amber, coffee and a cool climate.

points.title: Indigenous villages
points.text: Villages such as San Juan Chamula and Zinacantán have distinctive dress, religious practices and markets.

points.title: The Sumidero Canyon
points.text: A boat trip through a river gorge with crocodiles, monkeys and towering cliffs.

attractionsIntro: Palenque takes half a day, San Cristóbal two, and the waterfalls and canyon a day each.

attractions.name: Palenque archaeological site
attractions.text: A jungle Maya city with the Temple of the Inscriptions, the Palace with its tower, the Temple of the Sun and the Cross Group, many with stucco reliefs and inscriptions.
attractions.tip: Go at opening, and stay for the forest sounds.

attractions.name: Agua Azul and Misol-Ha

image.alt: The turquoise cascades of Agua Azul in Chiapas

attractions.text: A series of turquoise, terraced waterfalls on the road between Palenque and San Cristóbal, and the tall Misol-Ha waterfall with a swimming pool at its base.
attractions.tip: Swimming is limited at Agua Azul in the rainy season.

attractions.name: The Sumidero Canyon

image.alt: The steep walls of the Sumidero Canyon above the Grijalva River

attractions.text: A 1,000-metre-deep canyon carved by the Grijalva River, explored by boat from Chiapa de Corzo, with crocodiles, spider monkeys and birds.

attractions.name: San Cristóbal's centre and markets
attractions.text: A colourful town of tiled roofs, plazas and the Santo Domingo church and craft market, with amber and textile shops.

attractions.name: San Juan Chamula and Zinacantán
attractions.text: Tzotzil Maya villages near San Cristóbal, with a church interior where indigenous ritual mixes with Catholicism, and weaving traditions.
attractions.tip: Photography inside the church is prohibited. Go with a local guide.

attractions.name: Toniná and Bonampak
attractions.text: Less visited Maya sites, Toniná with a large pyramid and Bonampak with vivid murals.
attractions.tip: Combine with a Lacandon jungle trip.

thingsToDoIntro: Chiapas repays time and a sense of adventure.

thingsToDo.title: Explore Palenque at opening
thingsToDo.text: Walk the temples, then follow jungle paths to smaller groups and a waterfall.

thingsToDo.title: Swim at Misol-Ha and Agua Azul
thingsToDo.text: Cool off in waterfall pools on the way between Palenque and San Cristóbal.

thingsToDo.title: Take a boat through the Sumidero
thingsToDo.text: A two-hour trip through the gorge, with wildlife and cliff views.

thingsToDo.title: Visit indigenous villages respectfully
thingsToDo.text: Chamula and Zinacantán give a glimpse of living Maya traditions.

thingsToDo.title: Drink Chiapas coffee
thingsToDo.text: Highland coffee is among the best in Mexico, served in cafés in San Cristóbal.

thingsToDo.title: Shop for amber and textiles
thingsToDo.text: Chiapas amber and hand-woven cloth are sold in the town's markets.

foodIntro: Chiapas food is hearty and distinctive, with local corn, beans, chiles and coffee.

foods.name: Cochito and tamales
foods.text: Roast pork in an adobo sauce, and large tamales of chipilín herb.

foods.name: Pozol
foods.text: A cold drink of fermented corn dough, sold at markets.

foods.name: Chiapas coffee and chocolate
foods.text: Locally grown coffee and hot chocolate.

foods.name: Fresh river fish
foods.text: Grilled fish, served in Palenque and Chiapa de Corzo.

foods.name: Posh (pox)
foods.text: A traditional sugar-cane spirit used in rituals.

accommodation.intro: San Cristóbal and Palenque are the two bases, with a range of prices.

areas.name: San Cristóbal centro
areas.text: Hostels, guesthouses and boutique hotels in colonial houses.

areas.name: Palenque and El Panchán
areas.text: Jungle lodges and cabañas near the ruins, from basic to comfortable.

gettingThere.intro: Chiapas is about 1,000 km south-east of Mexico City.

options.text: Direct flights from Mexico City (1 hour 45 minutes), then a one-hour drive to San Cristóbal.
Overnight buses run from Oaxaca (about 10–12 hours) and Mexico City, and between San Cristóbal and Palenque (about 5–6 hours).
options.detail: Prefer daytime buses for scenery and safety.

options.text: The Tren Maya connects Palenque with Yucatán destinations.

gettingAround.intro: Colectivos, tours and taxis link the sites.

options.text: Shared vans link Palenque with Agua Azul and Misol-Ha, and San Cristóbal with the villages.
Day tours from San Cristóbal visit the Sumidero, Chamula and Zinacantán.

bestTime.headline: November–April
bestTime.summary: Palenque is hot and humid all year, and San Cristóbal is cool. The dry season is best for waterfalls and roads.

seasons.text: Dry and cool in the highlands, comfortable in the jungle.
Hot and dry in the lowlands.
Heavy rain, muddy roads, and waterfalls at their most powerful.
The end of the rains, green and fresh.

bestTime.avoid: The wettest months for road travel, and any period of blockades.

itinerary.title: Four days in Chiapas
itinerary.intro: Palenque and the waterfalls, then the road to San Cristóbal and the highlands.

days.title: Waterfalls to San Cristóbal
days.afternoon: The mountain road to San Cristóbal.

days.title: The Sumidero Canyon
days.afternoon: A boat trip in the canyon.

tipsIntro: Chiapas is remote and rewarding, and a few tips help.
tips: Check your government's advice for Chiapas, and local news for roadblocks.
Travel by day, particularly on mountain roads.
Bring warm clothes for San Cristóbal, and repellent for Palenque.
Ask before photographing people, and never photograph inside Chamula's church.
Carry cash, as ATMs are scarce.

faq.a: The main tourist areas, Palenque and San Cristóbal, are widely visited, but Chiapas has had unrest, road blockades and, in some areas, violence. Some governments advise caution. Check advice and local news, and travel by day.

faq.q: How many days do you need?
faq.a: Four or five for Palenque, the waterfalls, the Sumidero and San Cristóbal.
A 1994 armed uprising in Chiapas by an indigenous movement demanding land and rights. It is now mostly political, and Zapatista communities exist, but San Cristóbal is peaceful.

faq.q: Can I swim at Agua Azul?
faq.a: In some pools, in the dry season. Currents can be strong, and after rain the water may be brown.

faq.q: What is the best time to visit?
faq.a: November to April, though the rainy season is green and quiet.

faq.q: How do I get from Palenque to San Cristóbal?
faq.a: By bus or colectivo, about 5 to 6 hours, with a stop at the waterfalls.
